cell-compartmentalization-s1.title: Two enzymes across a range of pH
cell-compartmentalization-s1.text: Researchers purified two enzymes from liver cells: one found inside lysosomes and one found in the cytosol. They measured each enzyme's activity in buffers from pH 3 to pH 8, using the same amount of enzyme, the same amount of the molecule it breaks down, and 37 °C for every test. Activity is shown as a percent of each enzyme's highest activity; each point is the mean of three trials. The inside of a lysosome is about pH 5 and the cytosol about pH 7.2.

cell-compartmentalization-s2.title: Where the membrane is in two cell types
cell-compartmentalization-s2.text: Using electron micrographs, researchers estimated how a cell's total membrane area is divided among its membranes. Values are approximate percents of all the membrane in one cell, rounded from published electron-microscope measurements.

table.caption: Share of total membrane area (%) in a liver cell and a pancreas cell that secretes digestive proteins

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the lysosomal enzyme?
options: It is most active near pH 5 and works at about one-eighth of that at pH 7.
It is most active near pH 7 and works poorly in acidic conditions below pH 5.
It works equally well across the whole range from pH 3 to pH 8.
It is most active at pH 3 and loses activity steadily as pH rises.

why.correct: The lysosomal curve peaks at 100% at pH 5 and drops to 12% at pH 7, about one-eighth of its peak.
options: Correct: 100% at pH 5, 12% at pH 7.
That describes the cytosolic enzyme, which peaks at pH 7.
Activity ranges from 4% to 100%, so it changes a great deal with pH.
At pH 3 the enzyme is at 35%; it rises to its peak at pH 5 before falling.

items.q: If a lysosome leaks a few of its enzymes into the cytosol, the cell usually suffers little damage. Which explanation do the data support?
options: At the cytosol's pH of about 7.2, the lysosomal enzyme works at a small fraction of its top rate.
The cytosolic enzyme breaks down the leaked lysosomal enzyme as soon as it reaches the cytosol.
The lysosomal enzyme becomes more active at pH 7.2, but the cytosol contains nothing it can break down.
The cytosol is more acidic than the lysosome, so the leaked enzyme is quickly destroyed by the acid.

why.correct: The lysosomal enzyme is at 12% at pH 7 and lower above it. Keeping it in an acidic compartment lets it work there, while the neutral cytosol all but switches it off if it escapes: a built-in safety feature of compartments.
options: Correct: the pH difference between the two compartments protects the cytosol.
The data show activity versus pH; nothing in them shows one enzyme breaking down the other.
Activity falls from 100% at pH 5 to 12% at pH 7, so it becomes less active in the cytosol, not more.
The cytosol (pH 7.2) is less acidic than the lysosome (pH 5), not more.

items.q: How many times more active is the lysosomal enzyme at pH 5 than at pH 7? Give your answer to one decimal place.

why.correct: 100% ÷ 12% ≈ 8.3. Moving the enzyme from the lysosome's pH to the cytosol's cuts its activity more than eightfold.

items.q: A drug blocks the proton pumps in lysosome membranes, so the inside of the lysosomes rises from pH 5 to pH 7. Which effect is most likely?
options: Material taken into lysosomes is broken down much more slowly, so it builds up inside them.
Material in lysosomes is broken down faster, because the cytosolic enzyme now works inside them.
The lysosomal enzymes leak out and begin digesting the cytosol at their highest rate.
Lysosomes work as before, because their enzymes are protected by the lysosome membrane.

why.correct: At pH 7 the lysosomal enzymes work at about 12% of their peak, so digestion inside the lysosome slows sharply and undigested material accumulates.
options: Correct: losing the acidic condition cripples the enzymes that need it.
The cytosolic enzyme is not inside the lysosome; raising the pH does not move it there.
The drug changes pH, not the membrane's integrity; and at pH 7 the enzymes would be weak even if they leaked.
The membrane keeps the enzymes in, but it is the acidic pH inside, which the pumps maintain, that lets them work.

items.q: Why did the researchers use the same temperature and the same amounts of enzyme and of the molecule being broken down at every pH?
options: So pH was the one factor that differed, and any change in activity could be traced to it.
So that the enzymes would work at their highest activity in each test, regardless of the pH.
So that the lysosomal and cytosolic enzymes would give the same results and could be averaged.
So that the experiment needed no repeated trials, because nothing could vary between tests.

why.correct: pH is the independent variable. Holding everything else constant (controlled variables) means differences in activity can be attributed to pH alone.
options: Correct: controlled variables keep other factors from explaining the pattern.
Activity still changed a great deal with pH; controlling other factors does not hold activity at its peak.
The two enzymes behaved very differently, which is the point of comparing them; they were not averaged.
Random variation still occurs, which is why each point is a mean of three trials.

items.q: What share of the liver cell's membrane is inside the cell rather than at its surface?
options: About 98%
About 35%
About 2%
About 50%

why.correct: The plasma membrane is the only surface membrane, at 2%. Everything else, 100 − 2 = 98%, is internal membrane.
options: Correct: all but the plasma membrane's 2% lies inside the cell.
35% is the rough ER alone, just one of the internal membranes.
2% is the plasma membrane, the surface; the question asks about the inside.
The internal membranes add up to far more than half: rough ER and mitochondrial inner membrane alone are 67%.

items.q: In the liver cell, how many times larger is the area of the inner mitochondrial membrane than the outer one? Give your answer to one decimal place.

why.correct: 32% ÷ 7% ≈ 4.6. The inner membrane wraps the same organelle as the outer one, yet has almost five times the area.

items.q: Which feature of mitochondria explains the result of the previous calculation, and why does it matter?
options: The inner membrane is folded into cristae, packing in more area for the membrane proteins that make ATP.
The inner membrane is thicker than the outer one, so it shows up as more area in electron micrographs.
Each mitochondrion holds several inner membranes stacked inside one outer membrane, like nested boxes.
The outer membrane has been partly lost in liver cells, so the inner membrane is left to do its job.

why.correct: The inner membrane folds back and forth into cristae. Folding packs far more membrane, and so far more of the proteins that make ATP, into the same small organelle.
options: Correct: folding, not size, gives the inner membrane its extra area.
Thickness does not change area; area is measured along the membrane's surface.
There is one inner membrane, heavily folded, not several separate ones.
Liver mitochondria have intact outer membranes (7% of the cell's membrane).

items.q: Which claim about the pancreas cell is best supported by the table together with what you know about organelles?
options: It is specialized for making and exporting proteins, since rough ER and Golgi make up 70% of its membrane.
It is specialized for making lipids, since its smooth ER is the largest share of its membrane.
It makes more ATP than the liver cell, since its mitochondrial membranes are a larger share of the total.
It takes in more material from outside than the liver cell, since its lysosome membranes are the largest share.

why.correct: Proteins for export are made on rough ER and processed in the Golgi. Their membranes are 60% + 10% = 70% of the pancreas cell's total, much more than in the liver cell (42%).
options: Correct: a huge share of rough ER and Golgi fits a cell that secretes digestive proteins.
Smooth ER is only 1% in the pancreas cell; it is the liver cell that has much more (16%).
Mitochondrial membranes are 21% in the pancreas cell against 39% in the liver cell, a smaller share, not a larger one.
Lysosomes are grouped with other small membranes at 3%; nothing in the table singles them out.

items.q: Which statements are supported by the table? Select all that apply.
options: In both cells, the rough ER has more membrane than any other single membrane.
The liver cell has a larger share of smooth ER than the pancreas cell.
The plasma membrane is the largest membrane in the pancreas cell.
The pancreas cell's mitochondrial membranes add up to more than its rough ER.
The two cells divide their membranes among organelles in the same way.

why.correct: Check each statement against the numbers; two match.
options: Rough ER is 35% in the liver cell and 60% in the pancreas cell, the largest single entry in each.
Smooth ER is 16% in the liver cell against 1% in the pancreas cell.
The plasma membrane is 5% of the pancreas cell's membrane, one of the smallest shares.
Its mitochondrial membranes total 4% + 17% = 21%, far less than its 60% rough ER.
The shares differ a lot, for example smooth ER (16% against 1%) and rough ER (35% against 60%).

items.q: What is the nucleoid of a prokaryotic cell?
options: The region where its DNA is concentrated, with no membrane around it
A membrane-bound sac that holds its DNA, like a small nucleus
A cluster of ribosomes where the cell builds its proteins
The thick outer layer of the cell wall that protects the DNA

why.correct: A nucleoid is a region, not an organelle: the DNA gathers there, but no membrane separates it from the rest of the cytoplasm.
options: Correct: a DNA-rich region without a surrounding membrane.
A membrane-bound DNA compartment is a nucleus, which prokaryotes lack.
Ribosomes are scattered through the cytoplasm; the nucleoid is where the DNA is.
The cell wall is outside the plasma membrane and holds no DNA.

items.q: Liver cells build fatty acids in the cytosol and break fatty acids down inside mitochondria. Why is it useful that these happen in different compartments?
options: Keeping them apart stops new fatty acids from being broken down straight away, wasting energy.
Keeping them apart lets both processes use the same enzymes, which saves the cell from making extra proteins.
Keeping them apart means the fatty acids can be built and broken down at the same rate in each compartment.
Keeping them apart lets fatty acids leave the cell faster, because each compartment opens to the outside.

why.correct: Building and breaking down the same molecule in one space would undo each other in a pointless, energy-wasting cycle. Separate compartments let the cell control each process on its own.
options: Correct: separating opposing processes keeps them from cancelling each other out.
Building and breaking down use different sets of enzymes; separation is not about sharing enzymes.
The point is to control them separately, not to make them equal in rate.
The cytosol and mitochondria do not open to the outside of the cell.

items.q: A student claims that because prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles, their insides have no organization at all. Which observation best refutes the claim?
options: Their DNA gathers in a nucleoid, and some have internal membrane sheets for photosynthesis.
Their cytoplasm contains ribosomes, which are made of rRNA and protein and build the cell's proteins.
Their plasma membrane contains transport proteins that control which substances enter and leave.
They are usually much smaller than eukaryotic cells, so substances reach each part of the cell by diffusion.

why.correct: A DNA-rich nucleoid and specialized internal membranes are regions set aside for particular jobs: organization without membrane-bound organelles.
options: Correct: the nucleoid and internal membrane folds show specialized regions inside prokaryotes.
Having ribosomes is true of all cells; it does not show that parts of the cell are set aside for particular jobs.
This describes the surface membrane, not organization inside the cell.
Small size explains why prokaryotes manage without organelles; it does not show internal organization.

items.q: Order these compartments of an animal cell from most acidic to least acidic.
options: Lysosome interior (about pH 5)
Cytosol (about pH 7.2)
Mitochondrial matrix (about pH 7.8)

why.correct: Lower pH means more acidic. The lysosome (about 5) is most acidic, then the cytosol (about 7.2), then the mitochondrial matrix (about 7.8), which is slightly basic. One cell holds all three at once because membranes keep them apart.

items.q: Chloroplasts hold their light-absorbing proteins in thylakoids, flattened membrane sacs piled into stacks. What advantage does this arrangement give?
options: It packs a large membrane area into the chloroplast, so it holds many more light-absorbing proteins.
It keeps light out of the stroma, so the reactions there can run in the dark at any time of day.
It lets the chloroplast take in water faster, because each thylakoid works like an aquaporin.
It makes the chloroplast smaller, so it can move to the cell surface where light is strongest.

why.correct: As with the cristae of mitochondria, folding and stacking membranes multiplies the area available for membrane proteins in a small space.
options: Correct: more membrane area means room for more of the proteins that capture light.
Stacking thylakoids does not shade the stroma; its job is to add membrane area.
Thylakoids are not water channels; water crosses membranes through aquaporins.
Stacking packs in membrane without shrinking the chloroplast, and chloroplast position is a separate matter.

items.q: Certain cells cannot make a working version of the lysosomal enzyme that breaks down a particular fat. Which outcome is expected in these cells?
options: That fat builds up inside their lysosomes, which swell, while other lysosomal digestion continues.
That fat is broken down in the cytosol instead, because the cytosolic enzymes take over the job.
Digestion in their lysosomes stops altogether, because lysosomes need each of their enzymes to work.
That fat leaks out of the lysosomes and is digested by the acidic contents of the cytosol.

why.correct: Each lysosomal enzyme breaks down particular molecules. Without the one for this fat, the fat is delivered to lysosomes but not digested, so it piles up there. Inherited conditions of this kind are called lysosomal storage diseases.
options: Correct: the undigested molecule accumulates in the compartment where it should have been broken down.
Cytosolic enzymes are different enzymes; they do not take over a specific lysosomal job.
The other lysosomal enzymes still work on their own targets; only this fat's breakdown fails.
The cytosol is not acidic (about pH 7.2), and it does not digest fats this way.

items.q: Which are advantages that internal membranes give a eukaryotic cell? Select all that apply.
options: Different pH and other conditions can be kept in different organelles at the same time.
Opposing processes, such as building and breaking down a molecule, can be kept apart.
Membrane folds pack extra area for membrane proteins into a small space.
Molecules move between organelles faster than they would if the cell were one open space.
Each reaction in the cell can then run at the same pH and temperature.

why.correct: Compartments separate conditions, separate opposing processes and, through folding, add membrane area. They do not speed up movement between compartments, and the whole point is that conditions differ.
options: Separate conditions, such as the acidic lysosome inside a neutral cytosol, are a key advantage.
Separating opposing processes keeps them from undoing each other.
Cristae and thylakoids are folds that add membrane area.
Membranes are barriers; moving between organelles takes transport or vesicles, which is slower than open diffusion.
Compartments let conditions differ from place to place; they do not make them all the same.

items.q: A cell must keep a reaction's starting molecules at high concentration to make the reaction run fast. How can a membrane-bound compartment help, even in a large cell?
options: Transport proteins can gather the molecules into a small space, where their concentration stays high.
The compartment's membrane makes the molecules react without any enzyme being present.
The compartment lets the molecules diffuse faster, because water moves more quickly inside organelles.
The compartment raises the cell's surface area-to-volume ratio, so the whole cell becomes smaller.

why.correct: Spread through the whole cytosol, the molecules would be dilute. Pumped or carried into a small compartment, the same number of molecules is far more concentrated, so they meet their enzymes more often.
options: Correct: a small, enclosed space keeps reactants concentrated where they are used.
Enzymes are still needed; a membrane does not speed up the reaction itself.
Diffusion is not faster inside organelles; the gain comes from concentration, not speed.
A compartment does not change the size of the whole cell or its outer surface area.

items.q: In a diagram, a cell has DNA surrounded by a double membrane with pores, ribosomes on membranes nearby, and small acidic sacs. Which kind of cell is it, and why?
options: Eukaryotic, because its DNA is enclosed in a nucleus and it has membrane-bound organelles.
Prokaryotic, because its DNA is in a nucleoid and it has ribosomes for making proteins.
Prokaryotic, because its double membrane and pores show a cell wall around the DNA.
Eukaryotic, because it has ribosomes, which prokaryotic cells do not have.

why.correct: A double membrane with pores around the DNA is the nuclear envelope; ribosomes on membranes mean rough ER; acidic sacs are lysosomes. Membrane-bound compartments mark a eukaryote.
options: Correct: a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles identify a eukaryotic cell.
A nucleoid has no membrane around it, but this DNA is enclosed by a double membrane.
A cell wall is outside the plasma membrane; a double membrane with pores around the DNA is a nuclear envelope.
Prokaryotes do have ribosomes, so ribosomes cannot tell the two kinds apart.

items.q: Eukaryotic cells are usually 10 to 100 times wider than prokaryotic cells. Which claim best links this to compartments?
options: Internal membranes add working surface and keep reactions concentrated in small spaces, helping a large cell function.
Internal membranes raise the surface area-to-volume ratio of the outer membrane, so large cells exchange faster.
Large cells need compartments to hold extra water, which keeps them from bursting in hypotonic solutions.
Compartments make cells larger by adding membrane, so having organelles is what causes eukaryotic cells to be big.

why.correct: In a large cell, the outer membrane is small compared with the volume, and molecules would be dilute if spread through it. Internal membranes provide extra surface for membrane proteins and small spaces where reactants stay concentrated.
options: Correct: compartments supply surface and concentration inside the cell, offsetting some costs of large size.
Internal membranes do not change the outer membrane's area or the cell's volume, so its surface area-to-volume ratio is unchanged.
Compartments are not water stores for preventing bursting; water balance is a separate matter.
This reverses cause and effect; adding membrane does not by itself make a cell larger.
